content.thinking:
I'm piecing together the postmortem record: the revert of the monthly-spend-feature was refuted while the legacy-checkout-fallback revert was confirmed, meaning the lead's original call was correct and the investigator's refutation was mistaken. But I'm also noticing the logs showing repeated ZeroDivisionError occurrences at spend_summary.py:47, which complicates that conclusion.

Looking at the flag-off rollout percentages for both the legacy-checkout-fallback and monthly-spend flags, I see both hover suspiciously close to the observed error rate (~29-30%), making it ambiguous which flag actually drives the error. I can't prove causation cleanly, but I lean toward hypothesizing that disabling legacy-checkout-fallback routes traffic to a new renderer path that hits the spend_summary error, while being careful to flag this as an unproven assumption rather than a confirmed root cause.

Building the causal chain now: users hit failing account pages with elevated error rates during the incident window, traced to the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, which traffic reached only because legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off and shifted requests onto the new path. The toggle itself was done without any guard, canary, or alert on flag changes, which I'm flagging as a contributing factor alongside the unguarded divide-by-zero in the code.

I'm confirming the fix was a revert of M2, then outlining contributing factors: the investigator initially pursued the wrong lead since two flags changed within seconds of each other making attribution hard, so I'm proposing action items to treat concurrent flag changes as joint candidates, stagger/annotate flag toggles, add a guard to the fix, and require testing the legacy path with the flag off before removal — numbering these as AI-3 onward.

I'm also noting a detection gap: the alert fired noticeably after the incident actually began, so I'm adding alert lag as a contributing factor and considering whether to fold it into an AI-6 action item for faster detection.

On the lead side, L1's hypothesis wasn't acted on initially since Argus reverted the other flag first and M1 refuted it, but ultimately M1's correction led back to L1's original call being proven correct, so I'm framing this as "didn't change the first action, but vindicated by the outcome." I'm also computing the time wasted between M1 being raised and refuted using the two timestamps, and then drafting the executive summary in plain prose without specific figures, just naming the key actors and events.

action_items.item: Require flag changes in production to be made one at a time, each announced in the change feed and the incident channel, so that a regression can be tied to a single toggle.

Change the Investigator so that, when more than one flag changed shortly before onset, each is kept as a candidate until it is tested. A named lead from the thread should be weighed against the flag-change history, not dismissed because a different error appears in the logs.

Before the fallback is retired, test the account-page path with legacy-checkout-fallback off in a pre-production or canary environment. Switching it off in production should be a gradual rollout with an error-rate guard.

causal_chain.step: Users saw account pages fail. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}, between {began} and {recovered}. The service's own warning log showed the account-page error rate climbing.

The failing requests died with a ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47. Those errors appear from the onset and are the new failure; the ClientDisconnected errors are low-rate and were already there.

Those requests reached the failing code because legacy-checkout-fallback was off. Flag evaluations from the onset show the flag off for part of the traffic, and it stayed off afterwards. Restoring it to on brought the service back to baseline and stopped the paging rule. Reverting the other flag, monthly-spend-feature, had no effect. The record shows the effect but not the mechanism, so how the fallback being off leads into spend_summary.py:47 is an inference.

The flag was switched off by an admin as a production change shortly before the incident was handled. A second flag, monthly-spend-feature, was switched on seconds later. Nothing in the record shows the fallback being off was checked as safe, or that the two changes were kept apart.

contributing_factors.factor: Two flags were changed within seconds of each other, so the change that mattered could not be told apart from the one that did not. Argus acted on the wrong one first.

The investigation ruled out the flag a person had named. It treated the ZeroDivisionError as proof that the other flag was the cause and did not weigh both recent flag changes as candidates. The wrong flag was reverted first and the recovery was delayed.
The legacy fallback could be switched off in production without any check that the traffic it carries is safe on the other path. The code at spend_summary.py:47 divides by zero unguarded.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, a large share of requests to the shop's account pages failed. The error rate went from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. It began when a configuration switch that keeps a legacy checkout fallback in use was turned off. A second switch was changed within seconds of it. Argus first undid the second switch, which did nothing. It then restored the legacy fallback, and the errors stopped. A person had named that switch in the incident thread before any action was taken, and the automated investigation had wrongly ruled it out. A draft code fix for the underlying defect is open for review.

lead_effects.effect: It did not change the first action, because the investigation refuted it and Argus reverted monthly-spend-feature first. After that revert failed, Argus restored legacy-checkout-fallback, the flag L1 named, and that fixed the incident.

got_lucky: The fallback was a flag that could be switched back at once, so restoring it fully fixed the incident without a deploy. The ZeroDivisionError defect is still in the code and stays reachable until the proposed fix is merged.
went_well: Argus judged each action against the metrics. It saw that the first revert did not help and moved on, and it confirmed recovery only after the paging rule stopped firing.
The flag provider's history and the production change list made both flag changes visible quickly.
A draft pull request for the underlying code defect was opened right after mitigation.
went_wrong: The Investigator refuted the right lead and put the wrong flag first with high confidence. The first revert ran from {T18.1} to {T21.1}, which is {T21.1 - T18.1} spent before the right action began.
The alert was raised at {alert_raised}, which is {alert_raised - began} after the onset. The service was already failing before anyone was paged.
The recorded times of the two flag changes (P1, P2) are later than the onset and the first flag-evaluation log line (G7ad6). The record does not explain this.

input.root_cause: The feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off by an admin, and with it off a share of account-page requests reached the spend-summary code, which fails with a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47. Switching the flag back on cleared the errors. The record does not show why that code path breaks when the fallback is off.
